'''Elizabeth H. Roberts''' (born April 17, 1957) is an American politician who served as the 68th [[List of lieutenant governors of Rhode Island|lieutenant governor of Rhode Island]] from 2007 to 2015. A member of the [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic Party]], she served in that position during the administrations of [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] governor [[Donald Carcieri]] and [[Independent politician|Independent]]-turned [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrat]] [[Lincoln Chafee]]. She was elected in 2006, becoming the state's first female lieutenant governor and was succeeded by [[Daniel McKee]] on January 6, 2015. She later served as Secretary of Health and Human Services during the administration of Governor [[Gina Raimondo]], but subsequently resigned due to a widely criticized statewide computer system rollout.<ref name="Nesi" />

==Personal life==
Roberts graduated from [[Brown University]] in 1978 and earned an MBA in Health Care Management from [[Boston University]] in 1984.<ref name="RILTGV">{{cite web|url=http://www.ltgov.ri.gov/about/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100204015147/http://www.ltgov.ri.gov/about/|url-status=dead|archive-date=February 4, 2010|title=About Elizabeth Roberts|publisher=Rhode Island Office of the Lt. Governor|accessdate=November 26, 2019}}</ref> Prior to entering politics, Roberts has worked as a business strategy consultant, policy analyst, and health care manager.{{Citation needed|date=November 2019}} She resides in Providence, Rhode Island.<ref name="RILTGV"/>

==Early political career==
===Rhode Island State Senate===
Roberts served five two-year terms in the [[Rhode Island Senate]] from 1996 until 2006.<ref name="RILTGV"/> During her tenure in the state Senate, she was an activist for health and medical issues. Roberts also focused on economic development and job growth, and pushed for cleaner air and water, stronger schools, and increased attention to disaster preparedness.{{Citation needed|date=November 2019}}

During her tenure in the state Senate she served as the Chairwoman of the Senate Health and Human Services Committee. Later, she served as a co-chair of Permanent Joint Committee on Healthcare Oversight, which she used as a vehicle to push for reform for [[Blue Cross and Blue Shield]], the largest provider of health insurance in Rhode Island.{{Citation needed|date=November 2019}}

Roberts also helped expand the state's prescription drug program for seniors (RIPAE) and helped expand coverage to more families through Rite Care, the state's public health system. The reform organization [[Common Cause]] named Roberts one of the top two senators in Rhode Island in 2006, giving her the second highest rating in the General Assembly at 91% and an “A” for her reform efforts during the legislative session.{{Citation needed|date=November 2019}}

==Lieutenant governor==
Roberts was elected the state's first female lieutenant governor on November 7, 2006. She was inaugurated as the 68th lieutenant governor of Rhode Island on January 2, 2007. She toyed with the idea of running for [[Governor of Rhode Island|governor]] in the [[2010 Rhode Island gubernatorial election|2010 election]], but instead decided to run for re-election as lieutenant governor.{{Citation needed|date=November 2019}}

==Secretary of Health and Human Services==
After the [[2014 Rhode Island gubernatorial election|2014 election]] in which Roberts did not stand for election, Governor-elect [[Gina Raimondo]] announced Roberts as her nominee for the office of Secretary of the Executive Office of Health and Human Services.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.browndailyherald.com/2014/12/08/raimondo-taps-roberts-78-cabinet-position/|title=Raimondo taps Roberts '78 for cabinet position|last=Blum|first=Alexander|date=8 December 2014|work=Daily Herald|access-date=26 November 2019}}</ref>

===Computer system failure and resignation===
In February 2017, Roberts resigned from her post in the Raimondo administration.<ref name="Nesi">{{Cite news|url=https://www.wpri.com/news/health-secretary-elizabeth-roberts-resigns/|title=Health Secretary Elizabeth Roberts Resigns|last=Nesi|first=Ted|date=14 February 2017|work=CBS 12|access-date=26 November 2019}}</ref> She left the cabinet-level post for a variety of reasons, but the roll-out of the botched Unified Health Infrastructure Project (a new statewide computer network) overshadowed her tenure.<ref name="Nesi"/> The disastrous UHIP computer network launch in September 2016 saw scores of people without access government to programs such as food stamps and child care due to glitches in the software, designed<ref name="Deloitte">{{Cite news|url=https://www.providencejournal.com/news/20170217/ri-gov-raimondo-deloitte-ceo-discuss-state-computer-woes-at-calif-conference|title=R.I. Gov. Raimondo, Deloitte CEO discuss state computer woes at Calif. conference|last=Pina|first=Alisha|date=17 February 2017|work=The Providence Journal|access-date=26 November 2019}}</ref> by [[Deloitte]]. This crash created a backlog of over 20,000 cases.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://turnto10.com/i-team/nbc-10-i-team-ris-health-secretary-elizabeth-roberts-resigns|title=NBC 10 I-Team: RI's Health Secretary Elizabeth Roberts resigns|last=Davis|first=Katie|date=14 November 2019|work=NBC News|access-date=26 November 2019}}</ref>
